tldr: Instead of wiping viscous stains right away, this paper proposes a new paradigm: gathering stains into a single spot using segmented pushing actions before removing them. By separating 2D topological push planning from 3D surface tracking, it demonstrates strong zero-shot cleaning performance on unseen curved surfaces and different stain types without any additional training.
hero_caption: A comparison of cleaning results on ketchup and peanut butter using Full-Cover (FC), PushAll-Onetime (PO), and the proposed method (Push-Wiper). While conventional approaches spread the stain and cause secondary contamination, Push-Wiper reliably concentrates the stain at the center for clean removal.
overview:
In robotic surface cleaning, viscous stains like ketchup and peanut butter are notoriously tricky. They cannot be quickly soaked up like liquids, and wiping them with a regular sponge just smears them across the surface, causing secondary contamination. On the other hand, scrubbing with excessive force risks damaging the surface through frictional heat and mechanical stress.

To tackle this, the authors took inspiration from human behavior and devised a new "aggregate-then-finish" paradigm: gather the stain gradually into one spot before picking it up. Instead of solving complex fluid dynamics deformation models, they abstract the stain contour into a binary map and use a Diffusion Policy to generate step-by-step local pushing trajectories that minimize stain spread.

Furthermore, they completely decouple 2D topological push planning from actual 3D geometric execution. By combining an Arbitrary Surface Pose Interpolator (ASPI) with a hybrid force-position controller, the policy trained purely on planar surfaces directly adapts to arbitrary 3D curved surfaces.

In real-robot experiments, Push-Wiper improved the Cleaning Score (CS)—the percentage of stain area removed—by up to 130% compared to conventional full wiping and single-stroke pushing. Remarkably, despite being trained solely on planar data, it exhibited exceptional zero-shot generalization to unseen concave and convex surfaces, solid residues, liquid spills, and novel condiments without any additional training.
contributions: Reformulated viscous stain cleaning as a state aggregation problem and introduced an "aggregate-then-finish" paradigm using segmented pushing motions.
Established a decoupled system architecture separating low-frequency 2D macro planning via Diffusion Policy from 3D geometric tracking via ASPI and hybrid force-position control.
Demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization to unseen curved surfaces, solid residues, liquids, and unlearned viscous stains by abstracting visual textures and 3D geometry.

sections.heading: How to conquer viscous stains that spread the more you wipe?
sections.summary: While cleaning robots are expanding in domestic and commercial spaces, semi-solid, highly viscous stains like ketchup remain difficult to clean with conventional wiping or scrubbing. This paper proposes "Push-Wiper," reframing the problem as topological aggregation to gather stains into a single spot.
sections.details:
Automated cleaning robots are widely used for floors and windows in homes and commercial settings, but semi-solid viscous stains on tables remain a major bottleneck. Solid debris can simply be swept, and low-viscosity liquids can be absorbed with a sponge. However, viscoelastic materials like ketchup or peanut butter smear thinly across the surface when wiped with a sponge, causing secondary contamination that actually enlarges the soiled area.

Removing these requires applying enough tangential shear friction while maintaining adequate downward normal force. Unlike dishwashers that rinse with large volumes of water, table cleaning must work with limited liquid. Conventional scrubbing risks scratching surfaces, and naive single-stroke wiping merely scatters stains outward.

To solve this, the authors introduce Push-Wiper. Rather than explicitly solving complex fluid deformation models, it takes an "aggregate-then-finish" approach. In the gathering phase, a low-frequency Diffusion Policy plans step-by-step pushing trajectories from an abstract binary mask, using a sponge to herd the stain toward the center. In the post-processing phase, the collected cluster is lifted off, and the sponge cleans itself.

The real strength of this approach lies in completely separating 2D topological planning from 3D geometric execution. Thanks to this separation, the robot is not distracted by complex visual textures or 3D surface undulations, achieving remarkably strong zero-shot generalization.

sections.heading: Limitations of classical trajectory tracking and recent learning-based methods
sections.summary: Conventional robotic cleaning methods generally fall into classical control based on geometric coverage planning or learning-based approaches using RL and IL. However, neither manual-tuning-dependent classical methods nor learning methods tailored to single flat planes can flexibly handle complex viscous stains across diverse surfaces.
sections.details:
Research in robotic surface cleaning broadly splits into classical approaches and learning-based approaches.

Classical methods typically follow predefined coverage paths (like raster patterns) using position, impedance, or force control. While studies have explored contact constraints in whiteboard cleaning and hybrid force-position control with compliant arms for viscous stains, they still suffer from manual parameter tuning, frequent residues, and poor generalization. Every new environment or material requires delicate re-modeling and parameter adjustment.

On the other hand, recent learning-based methods largely rely on reinforcement learning (RL) or imitation learning (IL). Examples include wiping strategies acquired through RL or height adaptation combining force feedback and IL. Recently, Diffusion Policy—which has achieved remarkable results in robotics—has been paired with contact force control for whiteboard cleaning. However, these are confined to simple tasks like erasing marker ink on flat surfaces and cannot handle viscous stains that break apart and smear easily.

In short, classical methods are stable but fragile to environmental shifts, while learning methods offer flexibility but often overfit to narrow tasks. An integrated framework capable of handling diverse viscous stains across arbitrary curved surfaces at the same time has been missing.

sections.heading: Decoupling planning and control to realize "aggregate-then-finish"
sections.summary: Push-Wiper divides cleaning into a gathering phase and a post-processing phase. It generates macro pushing motions from a 2D binary mask via Diffusion Policy and executes them on arbitrary 3D surfaces using the novel ASPI interpolator and hybrid force-position control, achieving both contact stability and generalization.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The goal of Push-Wiper is to completely eliminate viscous stains from a surface. Discretizing the surface into a grid, stained cells are set to 0 and clean cells to 1. The framework defines an objective function to minimize the maximum spatial diameter $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{S}_{t})$ and the number of connected components $K(\mathcal{S}_{t})$, using segmented pushing actions $\tau$ to aggregate the stain into a compact cluster at the center ($\mathcal{D}<\epsilon, K \to 1$).

### III-B Gathering Phase
- **Action generation**: Rather than reasoning directly over raw RGB images, it observes an abstracted binary stain mask $\mathbf{M}_t$ stripped of texture. Because stains can be gathered in multiple ways depending on splatter patterns, a Diffusion Policy is used to model this multimodal distribution. Since contact occludes camera views and pushing drastically alters the stain shape, it operates as a low-frequency macro planner: observe $\to$ plan a single stroke $\to$ open-loop execution $\to$ re-observe. The action space is strictly constrained to 3 degrees of freedom on the plane: translation and yaw rotation $(x_b, y_b, \Delta\theta)$.
- **Trajectory generation**: The 3-DOF planar action is mapped to 3D curved surfaces by the proposed Arbitrary Surface Pose Interpolator (ASPI). ASPI projects planar points onto the 3D surface, retrieves surface normals $\mathbf{n}_m$, and aligns the tool's Z-axis to $-\mathbf{n}_m$. Using B-spline interpolation and trapezoidal velocity profiling, it generates smooth 6-DOF end-effector trajectories $\mathbf{P}_{traj}$ in real time. As a result, the policy never needs to learn 3D surface geometry.
- **Trajectory execution**: To ensure stable aggregation, a hybrid force-position controller incorporates an admittance controller maintaining a constant contact force (target normal force $F_z^{des} = 20\text{ N}$). The normal direction is force-controlled, while tangential directions and orientation are position-controlled. After each push stroke, the sponge is scraped against a spatula, and this loop repeats until the stain area drops below a threshold (100 pixels).

### III-C Post-processing Phase
Once the stain is concentrated in one spot, five predefined motion primitives are executed: "Dabbing" to press and lift the concentrated lump, "Scraping" to peel stain residue off the sponge, "Rinsing" in water, "Squeezing" against a mesh to drain water, and a "Final Wiping" pass across the surface. This enables the sponge to be self-cleaned, reused, and achieve complete removal.

captions.F2: The five motion primitives used in the post-processing phase: Dabbing to press and lift the stain lump, Scraping against a spatula, Rinsing in water, Squeezing to dehydrate, and Final Wiping along a dashed path, enabling automated sponge reuse.

sections.heading: Taming peanut butter! Zero-shot conquest of unseen curves and solids
sections.summary: Using ketchup and highly viscous peanut butter, Push-Wiper was compared against Full-Cover (FC) and PushAll-Onetime (PO). It outperformed baselines by up to 130% in cleaning score and transferred zero-shot to unseen convex/concave curves, liquids, and solid residues without any retraining.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The experimental system used a UR7e robot arm, a 6-axis force/torque sensor, a wrist-mounted RealSense D435 camera, and a sponge ($11\times 7\text{ cm}$) attached to a 3D-printed adapter. Tested stains included ketchup (viscosity $1000\sim 1500\text{ mPa}\cdot\text{s}$) and peanut butter, an ultra-viscous material roughly 20–30 times thicker ($29,452\text{ mPa}\cdot\text{s}$). The evaluation metric is the Cleaning Score (CS), defined as the percentage reduction in stained pixels before and after cleaning.

### IV-B Baselines and Training Conditions
Push-Wiper was compared against "Full-Cover (FC)," which wipes the entire area in a grid/zigzag pattern, and "PushAll-Onetime (PO)," which uses the same re-observation loop but attempts to sweep through the entire area in a single continuous stroke. Push-Wiper was trained purely on planar data: only 150 human-teleoperated tasks (448 push trajectories), expanded to 2,688 via affine augmentation.

### IV-C Cleaning Comparison of the Three Methods
Across 40 trials spanning different stains and difficulty levels, Push-Wiper achieved an average CS of **89.88**, an improvement of up to ~130% over FC (32.64) and PO (44.98). With peanut butter in particular, FC smeared the stain and aggravated secondary contamination (some trials yielded negative CS), while PO broke the stain apart with long strokes and scattered it. In contrast, Push-Wiper pushed progressively inward from the outside, stably condensing the stain at the center within a practical average time of 130 seconds.

### IV-D Zero-Shot Generalization to Unseen Surfaces
Using convex and concave testbeds never seen during training, tests were run with ketchup and peanut butter. ASPI dynamically adjusted end-effector orientation to surface normals in real time, yielding a CS of **91.45** on convex surfaces and **93.42** on concave surfaces—matching or exceeding planar performance.

### IV-E Generalization to Unseen Objects and Stains
Zero-shot tests were also conducted on a complex viscous stain (CVS, a blend of oyster sauce and black pepper sauce), a liquid spill (cola), and solid residues (five black wooden discs). For solids, gathering all pieces into one spot was marked as success (CS=100). Push-Wiper achieved CS 94.67 on liquid, CS 90.00 on solids, and CS 91.13 on CVS, mastering aggregation across vastly different physical regimes.

### IV-F Effectiveness of Post-Processing
Executing the post-processing primitives after gathering resulted in a CS of **100.00** (complete removal) for ketchup and **98.51** for peanut butter, confirming virtually spotless cleaning.

sections.heading: How topological aggregation charts a new course for general-purpose cleaning robots
sections.summary: This paper presented Push-Wiper, reformulating viscous stain cleaning into an aggregation problem solved by segmented pushing motions. By cleanly separating macro learning-based planning from force-position tracking control, it proved high cleaning scores and remarkable zero-shot generalization.
sections.details:
Push-Wiper resolves the secondary contamination dilemma inherent in conventional wiping through a fresh formulation: gather progressively, then collect. Separating topological planning over binary masks from geometric and force control via ASPI and hybrid force-position control serves as an excellent case study in how representation abstraction unlocks strong generalization in robotic manipulation.

Beyond improving CS by up to 130% over baselines, its ability to transfer zero-shot from planar training to unseen curved surfaces, liquids, and solid debris reveals immense potential for practical domestic and commercial service robots.

Future directions include incorporating collision avoidance constraints for human-shared environments and automatically optimizing post-processing workflows for an even broader variety of stain properties.

takeaways: When manipulating complex fluids and viscoelastic materials, abstracting visual observations into geometric topologies via binary masks yields far better generalization than relying on physical simulation.

Decoupling low-frequency 2D macro action planning (Diffusion Policy) from 3D constraint and force tracking (ASPI + admittance control) is the key enabler for zero-shot transfer to unseen curved surfaces.
For contact-rich, deformable tasks like wiping, repeating local discrete stroke optimizations with re-observation loops is vastly superior to single-pass end-to-end execution.
limitations: The post-processing phase (Dabbing, Scraping, Rinsing, etc.) relies on fixed, hard-coded motion primitives, leaving limited flexibility for varying stain volumes or container placements.
Stain buildup on the sponge flanks during the gathering phase (sponge saturation) is not dynamically mitigated through adaptive pushing angle adjustments.
No collision avoidance constraints with humans or obstacles are integrated, meaning additional safety control layers are needed before deploying in dynamic human-coexisting environments.
